CATHAY HOTEL SHANGHAI CHINA
FEB. 27, 1933
Dear Mr. Ball;
I promised you several days ago that I would write to you fully re
my converaation with darl Nahrmacher. He is a young man of about thirty three
years of age. He runs a garage to eat and sells, or tries to sell, air planes
to get rich. Todate he is not affluent. He represents Boeing as a
sort of sub-
agent under Gale and Company of this city, who are the recognized outlet for
United Aviation products in China. He also represents Fleet of Buffalo, and
claims to have sold about thirty training planes to the Chinese Government at
Nanking•
These are the planes being used by the American Aviation Mission at
Hangchow for the purpose of training Chinese Pilots. Nahmmacher has another
young fellow with him by the name of Lewis who is also a pilot. There is no
recognized civil aviation in China, no licenses are iasued for commercial or
private flying. Apparently both Nahmacher and Lewis have done a good deal
of
barnstorming
work by air all with a view of selling military,
rather than
private,
aircraft. He does not think there is any market over here for your
ships and is not really interested in having the agency. Nahmmacher is fairly
well regarded by the old timers over here. He is spoken of as a live wire, has
a good line of conversation - plenty of it - has lived over here long enough
to know his way around, and is reported financially responsible within some-
what restricted bounds.
Men who have lived over here for forty years frankly admit that they
do not know a bit more than when they came here, so you cant expect much from
a man who has been here two weeks.
There are a number of things with respect
to aviation, however,
which I am willing to write about. First, as I said be-
fore there is no civil aviation. landing fields are a long way apart, and you
would not have that picture of two crashes and a question mark hanging on the
wall
if the crackups had been over here. Your widow might have the first one.
Almost every inch of ground is taken up with rice fields - the Chinese pro-
nounce
"rice" "lice" and well they might when it comes to a forced landing,
for the fields are certainly "lousey". A big one is about the size of a tennis
court,
anicle deep in water,
surrounded with a ditch well dyked with a wall of
mud patted down by wet bare feet for a thousand years or so. Then where ever
there are no rice fields, you bump into an old Chinese custom. When & man or
woman dies the relatives carry the casket to a field and deposit said box on
top of the ground. There it must remain for one year. Then the relatives come
back and shovel dirt over the casket, thus making a mound. This remains there
as the nigger said about his sentence, from now on. Well you know there are a
few of these yellow fellows around, andthey just naturally keep on passing
out, with the result that graves are every where.
The whole country is wildly enthusiastic about aviation. Newspapers
headline the most trivial events, all the leaders fly, Gen. Chiang Kai Shek
and Marshal Chang Hsueh-liang each have their own tri-motored planes, the lat-
ter's personal pilot being Perry Hutton, an old Lambert Field barnstormer. It
is an expensive game over here.
They charge Frank Robertson prices even when
you buy gas in large quantities.
I personally, not to be quoted on any of
this letter,
think that the future of aviation over here is more or less tied
up with the operation of flying boats, and those operated by airlines only.
As you know air transportation has the best chance of successful operation
when it follows the
established trends and the habitual routes of trade. Here
surface transportation is almost all by boat. Automobile roads are few, quite
dangerous because of bandits, and where built are never maintained - the Chin-
ese never maintain anything. Their railroads are relatively unimportant.
the years to come when Aviation becomes much more reliable, and the necessity
for emergency fields less emphatic, it may be that land equipment will be more
practicable to operate.
Hope that I haven't bored you with thie long letter. I am feeling
fine, having & good time and love the work.
If Mies Ella or Mies Lane get un-
ruley just remember that I have turned out to be a d--- good typewritter and I
am used to
being dictated to - just ask Debby.
My very best to you alwaye and to Mrs. Ball,
Very sincerely
Sebs dear thought you might or intreated
in this leur to mr. Base.
potad
